\section{Related Work}
% This is to be removed in the end
% \begin{itemize}
%     \item cache-ext
%     \item s3-fifo
%     \item mglru
%     \item XRP: bpf in nvme layer
% \end{itemize}

% \textbf{IMPORTANT: ADD THIS SOMEONE PLS, ELSE I CRY}. Para about cache ext and eBPF.

Changing how Linux evicts pages has traditionally meant modifying and rebuilding kernel's memory-management code, a slow process: MGLRU took years to be merged upstream. eBPF removes this barrier by letting small, verified programs run inside the kernel at defined hooks, with BPF maps sharing state with user space. It is increasingly used to replace kernel policies rather than just observe them, as in sched\_ext for CPU scheduling. For our project, it means a device-aware eviction policy can be written, loaded and compared against existing policies without maintaining a custom memory-management patch.

cache\_ext \cite{cacheext} applies this idea to the page cache. Its modified Linux 6.6.8 kernel calls eBPF callbacks when folios are added, accessed and evicted, and when the kernel needs eviction candidates, so each cgroup can run its own eviction policy. Its authors implement eight policies and report up to 70\% higher throughput and 58\% lower tail latency than the default. Related frameworks make paging \cite{pageflex} and prefetching \cite{fetchbpf} programmable. None of these considers which device a cached page came from.
A similar eBPF-based extension is XRP\cite{xrp}, which lets applications run custom eBPF functions in the NVMe driver to issue chains of dependent reads, such as B-tree lookups, without passing back through the kernel storage stack. However, XRP\cite{xrp} bypasses the page cache and targets only NVMe devices, as opposed to \texttt{cache\_ext}\cite{cacheext}.

Existing policy work around page cache policies are Least-Recently-Used-(LRU)-like approximations that assume removing the least recently used page would prove beneficial. For example, the linux kernel uses MGLRU \cite{multigenlru}, which groups pages into generations by how recently they were accessed and uses a feedback controller that balances eviction according to page refault rate: it counts every refault the same, so a page re-read from a slow HDD weighs no more than a re-read from a fast SSD. Another example would be S3-FIFO \cite{s3fifo} that uses three simple FIFO queues -- it adds a ghost queue to identify recently evicted pages and give it a higher priority. Like MGLRU, S3-FIFO also minimizes the number of misses and does not take into account the cost of the miss. Both S3-FIFO and MGLRU are available as eBPF policies for \texttt{cache\_ext} and can be used as comparisons.

Cost-aware caching is not new. GreedyDual \cite{greedydual} gives each cached object a credit equal to its miss cost and evicts the lowest-credit object. Forney et al. \cite{forney} applied this to file caches over heterogeneous devices. They partitioned the cache per device and resized partitions to balance work across devices. However, they evaluated it only in simulation, with devices whose performance differed far less than SSDs and HDDs do today.

 Linux itself already weighs refaults by IO cost \cite{lrubalance}: since version 5.8, reclaim balances anonymous and file memory by their refault rates weighted by swappiness. That cost model, however, has one weight per LRU list, not per device, so file pages from an SSD and an HDD remain indistinguishable.

% Separately, research on mixing different SSD NAND cell technologies continues at various levels, as packing exponentially more state per cell degrades characteristics surrounding performance and reliability. This creating a clear trade-off between the former characteristics against current (SLC, MLC, TLC, QLC) and projected (PLC) capacity per unit cost \cite{ssd_cell_characterised}. Transaction-level-modelling (TLM) simulations by Takai et al. demonstrate that optimal performance cost ratios exist for specific applications. Unfortunately the simulator remains closed-sourced, and the trace-based approach is infeasible under the proposed project.



\section{Evaluation methodologies}

% \begin{itemize}
%     \item cache-ext workloads
%     \item fio
%     \item dm-delay
%     \item Lbench
%     \item storage shims

We will use cache\_ext's own workloads as a starting point, including its modified LevelDB driven by YCSB. Alongside these we will run fio microbenchmarks that re-read files placed on each device. Each workload runs in a cgroup whose memory.max is a fraction of its working set, which forces eviction.

Where real HDD+SSD hosts are unavailable, or to sweep the latency gap in a controlled way, we emulate a slow device. dm-delay adds a fixed, millisecond-granularity delay to every I/O on an existing device. null\_blk is a memory-backed block device whose completion latency can be set in nanoseconds.

If we can reserve a host that has the heterogeneous device configuration (like a HDD), using Disk Mimic will allow us to characterise the HDD for us to simulate it later on in our tests \cite{disk_mimic}.
% If a HDD is temporarily accessible, using Disk Mimic will allow us to characterise the HDD for us to simulate it later on in our tests \cite{disk_mimic}.
However, Disk Mimic only simulates the I/O scheduling (which we reason would model realistic HDD delay), meaning that we would need to expose a block I/O interface. While the code behind the project is closed source, the paper was written by UW-Madison, which motivates the potential to acquire the source code.

\section{Criticisms}

% \section{Criticisms and next steps}
% I dount we will get space for "next steps" so

% This is to be removed in the end: 
% \begin{itemize}
%     \item TMO? Argue that refault rate is not the correct metric? PSI? -> ?
%     \item Unstable foundations of eBPF based kernels -- https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3689031.3717497 -> done
%     \item the use of a shim -> done
% \end{itemize}

Refault \emph{count}, the signal behind both MGLRU and S3-FIFO, may be the wrong objective on heterogeneous hosts. Meta's TMO~\cite{tmo} argues that a fixed refault or promotion-rate target is flawed because its cost depends on the backing device, and instead uses Pressure Stall Information (PSI) to measure the time lost to resource shortage. We will therefore report PSI I/O stall time alongside miss ratio.


% shim
It is well known that the use of shims does not accurately capture the characteristics of a device. For example, adding a shim to the device to emulate an HDD device penalises all IO equally, as opposed to positioning time that would vary the performance of different requests in different manners. This is a limitation this project has due to the lack of specialised hardware.

% bpf problems.
Additionally, recent work by Zhong et al. \cite{depsurf} on the foundations of eBPF-based kernel extensions has shown how changes in the kernel’s dependency surface have caused eBPF programs to fail silently or work incorrectly. These mismatches come from source code changes, configuration options and compiler inlining. The page cache is a clear example: the folio change in v5.16 renamed hundreds of functions, and the kfuncs \texttt{cache\_ext} relies on have no stable interface, so our policy is tied to \texttt{cache\_ext}’s v6.6.8 kernel.
